newsitem.title: USA: USDA may accept 16 mln acres for CRP, analysts say.
newsitem.headline: USDA may accept 16 mln acres for CRP, analysts say.

text.p: U.S. Agriculture Department is likely to accept around 16 million acres of U.S. cropland for entry into the long-term Conservation Reserve this fall, analysts said.

Farmers offered 25.6 million acres during a month-long "sign up" in March. The department selected the winning bids based on annual rent asked by farmers and the environmental benefits that would come from taking a parcel out of production.
Agriculture Secretary Dan Glickman was scheduled to the results Thursday at 1000 EDT/1400 GMT.

It was commonly believed USDA would accept about 16 million acres, effectively adding five million acres to U.S. grain-growing and livestock-grazing land. Contracts on 21.5 million acres in the reserve expire Sept 30.
"My guess is it will be somewhere around 16" million acres, said private consultant Bill Lesher.
"I'm betting 16 or 17 (million acres), some middle ground," said John Schnittker, a private consultant.
A Senate Agriculture Committee staff worker said the common figure among his sources was 16 million acres. One grain-trade source said he expected 14 million to 19 million acres to be accepted.

In addition to an overall enrollment figure, USDA will provide a list of acreage accepted in each state, a spokesman said, and should be able to say how much is new to the reserve and how much is re-enrolled.
Slightly more than half of the expiring 21.5 million acres were in seven, predominantly wheat-growing, states -- Colorado, Kansas, Minnesota, Missouri, Montana, North Dakota and Texas.

Just as important as the the enrollment totals, the Agriculture Committee staffer said, would be the average cost per acre in annual rent and USDA's calculation of benefits to be gained from the land.
"I personally will be interested in how new acres there are," he said, although the figure would not be a perfect indicator of better environmental targeting.

Agriculture chairman Richard Lugar, Indiana Republican, said earlier this week that he expected to see the average rent, now about $50 an acre, to drop and for environmental benefits to rise. The Plains and Midwest would continue to dominate enrollment, Lugar said.
Created in 1985, the Conservation Reserve Program pays farmes an annual rent to take fragile land out of production for 10 years.
Glickman's announcement would set in motion the biggest turn-over of acreage in CRP history.
It also would meet a self-imposed deadline to notify farmers by the end of May and rebut skeptics who said USDA was months late with the sign-up and made far too much land eligible.

Environmental groups mostly were willing to wait for the CRP results before deciding if USDA met the challenge. One group argued for a slow start to replenishing the CRP to ensure the right land was chosen.
Grain industry groups warned against idling too much land when food demand was high.
Glickman says USDA will hold another CRP sign-up this year.
